checks.explanation: The judge ranks printed in Table 4 determine a correlation of $42/55\approx0.764$ with the human ranks. The Elo values give the same ranks, and the gaps between them are too large for integer rounding to change that calculation.
checks.demonstration: Table 4 orders the models by human rank $r_i=i$, for $i=1,\ldots,11$. Reading its Judge Rank column in that order gives $$s=(3,4,5,6,1,2,7,9,8,11,10).$$ There are no ties in either ranking, and $\sum_{i=1}^{11}(r_i-s_i)^2=52$. Therefore Spearman's formula gives $$\rho=1-\frac{6\cdot52}{11(11^2-1)}=\frac{42}{55}=0.763636\ldots,$$ which rounds to $0.764$. Computing Pearson correlation directly on these rank vectors gives the same value. For comparison, the table's question-answering (QA) accuracy ranking has squared rank displacement $16$ and hence correlation $51/55=0.927272\ldots$, reproducing the reported $0.927$. The smallest judge Elo gap is $5$ and the smallest human Elo gap is $7$, so rounding the displayed Elo values to integers cannot reverse any rank.
checks.repair: Report the judge correlation as $\rho=42/55\approx0.764$ when describing the eleven-model comparison in Table 4. The derivation above supplies the corrected value from both the rank column and the Elo column. The QA comparison still favors the QA metric because $51/55>42/55$. If $0.804$ was computed from another model set or from a distribution of fitted rankings, that statistic needs its own clearly specified population and supporting results; it cannot be the Spearman correlation of the displayed ranks.
checks.scope: This finding concerns the Spearman correlation attached to Table 4. It does not refute the human-preference collection or the fitted Elo scores. The process-score column contains a printed tie, so its separately reported correlation is not recalculated here from rounded values.

checks.demonstration: Let $S$ denote the paper's video-quality score and let $\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{PR}}$ denote its process-aware reasoning score, both on the reported $0$–$100$ scale. Table 37 gives Wan2.2-14B an overall $S=30.0$ on the shared evaluation set, while Table 41 gives $S=38.5$ in the extended evaluation, a difference of $8.5$ points. For the Human-Centric dimension, Tables 39 and 42 give $S=38.1$ and $54.8$, respectively, so the difference is $16.7$ points. Tables 38 and 42 likewise give $\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{PR}}=14.5$ and $26.4$, a difference of $11.9$ points. Even allowing an error of $0.05$ at each rounded endpoint, these differences are at least $8.4$, $16.6$ and $11.8$ points. The shared overall table uses $80$ cases per model; the extended table reports $428$ for Wan2.2-14B, within a benchmark containing $436$ cases. The Human-Centric cells use $9$ shared cases and, for Wan2.2-14B, $76$ extended quality cases or $77$ extended process-score cases. Different case sets can produce these shifts, but they do not make the reported point estimates agree within a few tenths.
checks.repair: Replace the blanket numerical-agreement statement with the observed comparison: the extended evaluation changes the absolute scores appreciably. Across the six open-source generators, the largest absolute overall quality change is $9.3$ points for LongCat-Video, from $25.3$ to $34.6$. Across the four dimensions, the largest displayed process-score and quality changes are $11.9$ and $16.7$ points, both for Wan2.2-14B on Human-Centric cases. These values follow by subtraction from every corresponding cell in Tables 37–39 and 41–42, so this correction is sufficient to correct the reporting claim without changing either table. A claim that differences are statistically negligible would require an analysis accounting for the different case sets and the uncertainty in their score differences.

checks.location: Appendix G Table13 RWKV-UNet row, Avg column
checks.claim: Mean IoU of the twenty displayed source scores is79.84.
checks.explanation: The twenty printed RWKV-UNet scores sum to $1586.49$, giving an unweighted mean of $79.3245\%$, not $79.84\%$. Two-decimal rounding cannot explain the difference. Nor can one alternative set of nonnegative dataset weights explain the table: a ten-row calculation, including RWKV-UNet, contradicts every common weighted arithmetic rule even after allowing rounding in both the component scores and Avg. This does not identify which reported entries need correction.
checks.demonstration: Let $q_j$ denote the printed IoU for dataset $j$. The twenty values, in the table’s order and in percent, are $$\begin{gathered}72.32,84.76,80.06,84.97,87.48,\\84.53,85.95,70.85,59.75,88.10,\\85.75,68.96,84.56,70.75,96.21,\\63.61,85.20,87.56,72.56,72.56.\end{gathered}$$ Hence $$\frac1{20}\sum_{j=1}^{20}q_j=\frac{1586.49}{20}=79.3245.$$ If each displayed $q_j$ differs from its unrounded value by at most $0.005$ percentage points, the true unweighted mean differs by at most $0.005$ as well. Its interval $[79.3195,79.3295]$ is disjoint from the rounding interval $[79.835,79.845]$ for the reported average. The U-Net row averages to $78.3075\%$, which rounds to its printed $78.31\%$. To test a common weighted arithmetic rule, let $i$ be a model's printed table rank, $X_{ij}$ its printed IoU on dataset $j\in\{1,\ldots,20\}$, and $a_i$ its printed Avg, all in percentage points. Suppose one set of weights $w_j\ge0$, with $\sum_jw_j=1$, averages the unrounded scores for every model. Allowing each printed input and Avg to differ from its unrounded value by $0.005$ gives $$\left|a_i-\sum_jw_jX_{ij}\right|\le0.005+0.005\sum_jw_j=0.01.$$ Choose the following signed model coefficients $y_i$, which are distinct from the nonnegative dataset weights $w_j$; set every unlisted $y_i$ to zero. Rank $1$ is RWKV-UNet. $$\begin{array}{r|r|r|r}i&y_i&i&y_i\\\hline1&38&59&21\\21&-12&64&-17\\27&-23&71&19\\44&24&76&-9\\55&-44&79&5\end{array}$$ Taking this signed combination and bounding its rounding error by $0.01\sum_i|y_i|$ gives $$\begin{aligned}\sum_i y_i a_i&\le\sum_jw_j\left(\sum_i y_iX_{ij}\right)+0.01\sum_i|y_i|\\&\le\max_j\sum_i y_iX_{ij}+0.01\sum_i|y_i|.\end{aligned}$$ Direct arithmetic on the printed rows gives $$\begin{aligned}\sum_i y_i a_i&=198.74,\\\max_j\sum_i y_iX_{ij}&=196.30,\\\sum_i|y_i|&=212.\end{aligned}$$ A common weighted mean would therefore require $198.74\le196.30+0.01(212)=198.42$, which is false. The contradiction concerns one weight vector shared across these rows; choosing weights for RWKV-UNet alone is not ruled out.
checks.repair: Regenerate the dataset columns and Avg from the same unrounded evaluation records and state the aggregation rule. If Avg is unweighted and the printed RWKV-UNet entries are retained, their mean is $79.3245\%$, rounding to $79.32\%$. One common set of nonnegative dataset weights cannot reconcile the printed table, so merely disclosing fixed weights is insufficient. A different statistic, such as model-dependent weighting, micro-IoU pooling with model-dependent union counts, or a nonlinear aggregate, must be defined explicitly and checked against the results. Recompute any ranking that uses the reconciled aggregate. The summaries do not identify corrected raw scores or ranks.
checks.scope: The printed RWKV-UNet row does not have unweighted mean $79.84\%$. The ten-row certificate also rules out one common nonnegative dataset-weight vector for the table, allowing $0.005$ percentage points of rounding in each input and Avg. It does not exclude model-dependent weights, micro-IoU pooling or nonlinear aggregation. It does not locate the erroneous entries, recover raw model outcomes, establish a corrected ranking or refute broader conclusions about U-Net variants.

The common-weight contradiction shows that a single alternative arithmetic weighting rule cannot reconcile the table's comparisons. checks.claim: Theorem 1 and parameters (7)
checks.explanation: The moment algebra does not establish existence of an $[0,1]$-valued process for unrestricted resolutions. At fixed positive $\sigma$, the renormalized mean-reversion parameter eventually becomes nonpositive. Even positive $\widetilde\kappa$ must be accompanied by inward drift at both boundaries, equivalently a target in $[0,1]$. The proof's explicit stability restriction must therefore be carried into the main construction; it does not support an arbitrary-resolution limit with fixed noise.
checks.demonstration: Let the initial graphon and target both be $1/2$, with $\kappa=\sigma=1$ and $N=2$. Equation (7) gives $\widetilde\kappa=-1/2$, $\widetilde\sigma^2=4$ and constant mean $m_t=1/2$. The formal variance equation in Appendix C.2 becomes $v'(t)=1-3v(t)$, $v(0)=0$, hence $v(t)=(1-e^{-3t})/3$. For $t>(\log4)/3$, this exceeds $1/4$, impossible for a random variable in $[0,1]$ with mean $1/2$. The drift also points outward at both boundaries. This example is excluded by Appendix C.2's stated positive-$\widetilde\kappa$ assumption: it exposes the missing restriction in the unrestricted construction, not a contradiction to that restricted lemma.
checks.repair: State a finite-resolution admissible parameter range. For $\kappa>0$, $\sigma>0$ and $\mu\in(0,1)$, put $c_N=\sigma^2(N^2-1)/2$ and $m_t=\mu+(m_0-\mu)e^{-\kappa t}$. The drift is $b_t(x)=\kappa\mu-c_Nm_t-(\kappa-c_N)x$. For a given cell, require $\widetilde\kappa>0$ and $0\le\kappa\mu-c_Nm_t\le\widetilde\kappa$ for all relevant times. A simple sufficient condition uniform over $m_0\in[0,1]$ is $0\le c_N<\kappa\min\{\mu,1-\mu\}$. It makes $b_t(0)>0$ and $b_t(1)<0$, with diffusion vanishing at the endpoints. The linear drift is Lipschitz and the square-root diffusion is one-half Hölder; the usual one-dimensional square-root SDE existence and uniqueness argument gives an invariant $[0,1]$ process under these boundary conditions. Its finite-cell moment equations follow by Itô's formula. This repair bounds $N$ at fixed $\sigma$; an unbounded-resolution family must change the noise scaling or the construction. It does not create the pointwise space-time-white-noise field that the paper itself calls formal.
checks.scope: The issue is the unrestricted finite-cell construction and resolution claim in arXiv v1, uploaded July 8, 2026. Appendix C.2 and the experimental choice already acknowledge a stability restriction. The conditional moment calculation in an admissible regime is retained; neither the displayed example nor this repair establishes a continuous graphon diffusion.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 1 uses the cellwise Jacobi SDE with Equation (7)'s resolution-dependent parameters. It is stated conditionally on a solution, but the surrounding construction and fine-resolution discussion do not state a range ensuring a graphon-valued process. Appendix C.2 does impose $\widetilde\kappa>0$, and the experiments choose a small noise scale to satisfy that condition.
checks.title: The renormalized diffusion needs resolution-dependent admissibility conditions
checks.whyItMatters: A resolution-independent construction needs an actual bounded diffusion at every claimed resolution, rather than only formal moment equations.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 1 and Equations (6)–(7); Appendix C.2, Lemma 2 and variance equation (77); Appendix G.1 stability choice.

checks.claim: Equation (15) reverse-time SDE
checks.explanation: For a decreasing-time Itô SDE, state dependence contributes the additional drift $-\partial_xa$. Equation (15) contains only $b-a\,\partial_x\log p_t$. The missing term cannot be absorbed into the ordinary density score as it is defined in the paper.
checks.demonstration: Take $N=1$, $\kappa=\sigma=1$ and $\mu=1/2$. The forward diffusion has drift $1/2-x$, covariance $x(1-x)$ and stationary uniform density, whose score is zero. In the increasing reverse clock $u=T-t$, Equation (15) therefore gives drift $x-1/2$. Its generator applied to $x^2$ is $2x(x-1/2)+x(1-x)=x^2$, so under the supposedly stationary uniform law it gives $d\mathbb E[X^2]/du=1/3$. A stationary law requires zero. Including the covariance derivative instead gives reverse-clock drift $1/2-x$ and generator $2x-3x^2$, whose uniform expectation is zero.
checks.repair: For an admissible forward diffusion with positive differentiable interior densities and the boundary conditions needed for time reversal, add $-\widetilde\sigma^2(1-2x)$ to the decreasing-time drift. Equivalently, in the increasing reverse clock use $-b_t(x)+\partial_xa(x)+a(x)\partial_x\log p_t(x)$. This follows from the reverse probability current and restores the uniform stationary control exactly. The correction requires the forward law and its score to be well defined; it does not repair inadmissible forward parameters or a score computed from the wrong transition density.
checks.scope: The missing covariance derivative affects Equation (15)'s marginal-preservation property even in an admissible constant-parameter regime. A valid reverse law also requires the forward density, score and boundary behavior used in the time-reversal argument.
checks.claimContext: Equation (15) reverses the cellwise Itô diffusion while keeping its Jacobi noise coefficient. The covariance is $a(x)=\widetilde\sigma^2x(1-x)$, so it varies with the state. The paper uses the ordinary marginal-density score and claims that the reverse process preserves the forward marginals.
checks.title: The reverse drift omits the derivative of the state-dependent diffusion covariance
checks.whyItMatters: The score term alone is insufficient to reverse an Itô diffusion whose noise amplitude depends on the state.

checks.demonstration: Take $N=100$, $\kappa=1$, $\sigma=0.005$, $\mu=0.45$ and deterministic initial mean $m_0=0.7$. Then $\widetilde\kappa=0.8750125>0$, and $\widetilde\mu_t$ changes from approximately $0.41428980$ to $0.45$. These targets remain inside $[0,1]$. The renormalized mean equation gives $\mathbb E[X_t]=0.45+0.25e^{-t}$. A fixed Jacobi semigroup with target $0.45$ and the claimed rate $\widetilde\kappa$ instead gives $0.45+0.25e^{-0.8750125t}$. checks.location: Proposition4.2; Appendix A.3 proof applying Lemma A.1
checks.claim: Ambient Lebesgue tube volume bounds feasibility probability of uniform actions rolled through dynamics, yielding exponential latent advantage.
checks.explanation: Uniform actions need not induce uniform trajectories in state-action space. With deterministic dynamics, their pushforward is typically concentrated on a lower-dimensional dynamics graph. A set with tiny ambient volume can therefore have rollout probability one. Lemma A.1's ambient-volume inequality cannot supply the probability bound used in Appendix A.3.
checks.demonstration: For every horizon $H$, take state space $[-1,1]^{100}$, action space $[-1,1]$ and dynamics that set the next state identically to zero. Impose no additional state or action constraints. The feasible trajectory set is $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{traj}}=\{0\}^{100H}\times[-1,1]^H$, compact of intrinsic dimension $H$ in ambient dimension $101H$. Every action sequence rolls out into this set, so $P_{\mathrm{action}}(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{traj}})=1$. A latent decoder producing a feasible trajectory also has probability one, satisfying the proposition's condition for every $\delta\in(0,1)$. The ratio is exactly one. For every fixed $c>0$, the claimed lower bound $(1-\delta)e^{cH}$ exceeds one for sufficiently large $H$. The thin ambient geometry and the large rollout mass hold simultaneously.
checks.repair:
Use a bound on the actual action-pushforward law. If an independently justified condition gives $0<P_{\mathrm{action}}(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{traj}})\le r_H$ and the latent feasibility probability is at least $1-\delta$, then the ratio is at least $(1-\delta)/r_H$. An exponential conclusion requires a valid exponential upper bound on the volume of the action preimage $\Phi^{-1}(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{traj}})$, or another distributional argument. An ambient-volume bound transfers only under an additional domination condition: if $P_{\mathrm{action}}\ll
u$, where $
u$ is normalized ambient volume, with density at most $K_H$, then $
u(\mathcal N_\epsilon(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{traj}}))\le e^{-cH}$ implies $P_{\mathrm{action}}(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{traj}})\le K_He^{-cH}$. Deterministic rollout measures generally do not satisfy this domination premise. State the comparison conditionally rather than infer it from intrinsic dimension alone.

review-neurips-2026-151963.title: Flash-KMeans: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact K-Means

checks.claim: Read all 43,689 cached characters through references. Checked Lloyd objective and exact assignment, FlashAssign online argmin and claimed IO costs, sort-inverse aggregation, asymptotic atomic count, out-of-core/tuning claims, reported latency and speedups.
checks.explanation:
No substantive demonstrated algorithmic defect; exactness verified in real arithmetic with floating-point aggregation caveats.

Online argmin is associative when ties are consistently resolved and all valid centroids are visited; a 103-point random test reproduces direct Lloyd assignments exactly. Sorting indices preserves membership and segment sums add to the same cluster sufficient statistics; count and sum comparison passes to roundoff. At most occupiedK+ceil(N/BN)-1 partial segments exist, establishing the stated O((K+ceil(N/BN))*d) atomic upper bound even when clusters are empty. Empty-cluster centroid policy is unspecified but a standard carry-forward or reseeding convention repairs division by zero. Exact means standard Lloyd/no approximate nearest-neighbor or coreset, not bit-identical floating point across summation orders.

Screening IO concern: the actual CTA loop scans C for each point tile, so absent cache reuse centroid traffic can be ceil(N/BN)*K*d. The paper explicitly qualifies the one-read claim as ideal streaming; it is a cache-fit/reuse idealization, not a proven unrestricted HBM bound. The robust guaranteed benefit is removal of the N*K distance intermediate. Screening contention concern: a hot cluster spanning chunks still receives multiple global atomic merges. Thus elimination should be read as reduction of the dominant per-token contention, consistent with the low-contention algorithm heading; no claim that all atomics vanish is needed for the speedups. These limitations are recorded, not promoted to algorithm counterexamples.

Printed latency ratios reproduce approximate21.2/6.3/10.5 speedups; 94.4% corresponds17.86x. Code URL is supplied but no implementation or H200 profiler was inspected, so effective precision, tie policy, actual cache reuse, fixed-centroid global accumulation between out-of-core chunks, and time-to-first-run methodology remain unverified. No empirical speedup was independently reproduced. Remaining gaps: no code/benchmark rerun, external revision search, or independent reviewer.

checks.contextBefore:
Computational tractability for solving (3).
In practice, the cost for solving (3) is negligible compared to the cost of generating reasoning traces and querying the judge model. Minimizing $H(\mathbf{x})$ over $\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{N}$ is NP-hard in general, since it is a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, which subsumes classical NP-hard problems such as Max-Cut (Lucas, 2014).
However, under our answer-level constraints, the feasible set is restricted to only $K$ configurations, each corresponding to a candidate answer group. Consequently, solving (3) reduces to evaluating the objective over $K$ candidates, yielding a time complexity of $O(K)$ and making exact optimization tractable at inference time. With the top- $\kappa$ approximation, the complexity further reduces to $O(\kappa)$ .
checks.contextAfter:
We evaluate Joint Consistency on heterogeneous traces from MathArena, where candidate solutions to the same problem are generated by diverse models. This setting captures a realistic crowdsourced scenario, in which traces differ in generator quality and typically lack shared intrinsic evaluation signals such as token-level log-probabilities or process rewards.
Thus, intrinsic-evaluation-based methods such as Self-Certainty, DeepConf, or PRM-based aggregation are not directly applicable.

review-neurips-2026-152678.title: GDMD: Guiding Distribution Matching Distillation with Gradient-Based Reinforcement Learning

checks.claim: Gradient-based scoring preserves the original descent direction.
checks.explanation: At the old policy, the preference gradient is a signed multiple of the base gradient, not necessarily a positive one. Away from the old policy there is also a policy-displacement term, so even collinearity is not automatic.
checks.demonstration:
Hold the target and reward fixed, as in the stopped-target formulation. Write \(d=v_\theta-v^{\mathrm{old}}\) and \(e=v^{\mathrm{old}}-v\). Equation (6) expands to
\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RL}}=\|e\|^2+2\beta(2r-1)\langle e,d\rangle+\beta^2\|d\|^2.\]
At \(d=0\), its output gradient is \(2\beta(2r-1)e\), whereas the base squared-error gradient is \(2e\). Take an identity scalar model with current and old output zero, target two, \(\beta=1/2\), \(r=1/4\), \(\lambda=0.1\), and \(\gamma=1\). Equation (5) realizes this reward with normalized reward difference \(-1/2\). The base, preference and joint derivatives are respectively \(-4,1,0.6\); gradient descent on the joint loss therefore reverses the base descent direction. Using a half-normalized base loss does not change the reversal.
checks.repair: Describe the objective as signed preference reweighting and qualify any alignment guarantee. For one sample at the old policy, the joint gradient under the squared-error convention is \(2[\lambda+\gamma\beta(2r-1)]e\), so its sign is preserved exactly when that coefficient is nonnegative. With nonnegative weights, \(\lambda\geq\gamma\beta\) is a sufficient condition for all \(r\in[0,1]\) at that point. This is not an aggregate-gradient guarantee: for a full update, require the actual condition \(\langle\nabla\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DMD}},\nabla\mathcal L_{\mathrm{GDMD}}\rangle>0\) for strict first-order descent of the DMD objective. Policy drift and differing sample weights must be accounted for separately.

checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. Re-derived the pure-state identity and the mixed-state extension. For real normalized components q_j and posterior weights w_j(x)=pi_j q_j(x)/q(x), score(q)=sum_j w_j score(q_j). checks.contextBefore:
On the other hand, improving LLM quality by scaling them up makes them more expensive, both in terms of raw computation (“compute”, measured in FLOPs) and dollars. The compute required to train an LLM is proportional to both the parameter count $n$ and training data budget $d$ , so scaling up both of these increases compute quadratically.
Inference compute scales with $n$ but not $d$ .
As $n$ and $d$ have jumped orders of magnitude, the compute required for training and inference have also increased exponentially.
While quality improvements are monotonic in these variables, they are also diminishing, leading to the question of whether doubling down on making training more expensive to chase vanishing quality improvements will make LLM training profitable in the long run.
checks.contextAfter:
In this paper, we address this open question by developing a theory of profit-optimal training behavior for LLM firms.
Under our model, the firm chooses their model size $n$ and training data budget $d$ .
Larger choices of $n$ and $d$ produce higher-quality LLMs, which increases demand for the LLM, allowing the firm to charge more per inference token.
On the other hand, larger choices of $n$ and $d$ incur additional training and inference costs, suggesting that there is some profit-optimal $n^{*},d^{*}$ , i.e., a choice of these variables that maximizes profit.
We characterize $n^{*},d^{*}$ as a function of exogenous variables like hardware efficiency (FLOPs/$), the parameter and data efficiency of LLM training methods, and various natural constants.

checks.location: Theorem 4.4, text:267; Appendix B.3 final telescoping, text:1394–1405
checks.claim: All positive learning rates satisfying the displayed upper caps give the displayed finite-horizon stationarity bound.
checks.explanation: With a fixed number of rounds and a positive adaptive-optimizer denominator, the algorithm makes arbitrarily little progress as both learning rates shrink. Upper rate caps do not justify a positive rate-independent descent coefficient.
checks.demonstration:
Take two identical deterministic clients with \(f_i(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}\), initialization \(x_0=1\), full participation \(N=M=2\), \(K=2\), and \(T=100\), with no weight decay (\(\lambda=0\)). The gradient and Hessian are bounded by one, so use \(L=G=\epsilon=1\), \(\sigma=0\), and the permitted heterogeneity bound \(\sigma_g=10^{-12}\). Set both learning rates to \(10^{-8}\); all displayed caps are satisfied.

Full participation cancels the stored-history terms. Each local gradient has magnitude at most one, so \(|G^{(t)}|\le2\eta_c\), and the AdaGrad update moves by at most \(2\eta_s\eta_c=2\cdot10^{-16}\) per round. The iterates stay within \(2\cdot10^{-14}\) of one, where the squared gradient is approximately \(1/2\). The claimed bound is instead
\[\frac{4(\sqrt2-1)}{100}+4(A_1\sigma_g^2+A_3)\approx0.01656854.\]
Both rates are strictly positive; the paper’s discussion of the degenerate zero-rate case does not remove this example.
checks.repair:
Retain the actual, justified descent coefficients. If a valid analysis establishes deterministic \(c_t>0\) and errors \(r_t\) satisfying
\[\mathbb E f(w^{t+1})\le\mathbb E f(w^t)-c_t\mathbb E\|\nabla f(w^t)\|^2+r_t,\]
then telescoping gives
\[\min_{t<T}\mathbb E\|\nabla f(w^t)\|^2\le\frac{f(w^0)-f^*+\sum_{t<T}r_t}{\sum_{t<T}c_t}.\]
The coefficients must retain the client-update scale, server rate and preconditioner bounds. Their sum cannot be replaced by \(T/4\) under upper learning-rate caps alone. This supplies the required form of a valid rate; it does not establish the printed rate or its corollary for the unchanged algorithm.
checks.scope: The finite-round theorem is false under its stated rate conditions. The counterexample does not concern empirical performance or the correctness of unrelated optimizer implementations.
checks.title: Arbitrarily small allowed steps contradict the finite-round convergence bound
checks.claimContext: Theorem 4.4 imposes upper bounds on positive client and server learning rates, then gives a leading stationarity term independent of either rate. Appendix B.3 obtains this by replacing its descent coefficient by a fixed constant.
checks.whyItMatters: A convergence guarantee must reflect how much progress its allowed step sizes permit in the stated number of rounds.
checks.verificationNote: The discussion after Theorem 4.4 excludes a degenerate zero rate; the counterexample uses strictly positive rates.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 4.4; Appendix B.3, descent coefficient and final telescoping; Algorithm 1

checks.location: Lemma B.7, text:1213–1225; Eq8 and Appendix B.1
checks.claim: The mean-square difference between the actual server pseudo-gradient G and the mean local gradient h has the stated variance-only bound.
checks.explanation: The learning-rate and local-step factors do not disappear when variance vanishes. A variance-only bound cannot control this deterministic scaling difference.
checks.demonstration:
Take two identical deterministic clients \(f_i(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}\), full participation, \(K=2\), initialization one, and \(\eta_c=10^{-8}\). Set the optional weight decay to zero. Stored-history terms cancel exactly. The normalized average \(\bar h\) is nonzero, and
\[\|G-\bar h\|^2=(2\cdot10^{-8}-1)^2\|\bar h\|^2>0.\]
Every term on the lemma’s right side vanishes: the stochastic variance is zero, and every participation-error term contains \(N-M=0\). Thus the printed inequality asserts that a positive deterministic quantity is at most zero.
checks.repair:
Choose a consistent scale throughout the analysis. Put \(a=\eta_cK\) and \(\widetilde G=G/a\). If the intended variance estimate concerns the normalized update, it must be proved for \(\widetilde G\) and consistently propagated through the stored states and adaptive update. For the literal unnormalized \(G\), the exact decomposition is
\[G-\bar h=a(\widetilde G-\bar h)+(a-1)\bar h,\]
so a valid general bound is
\[\mathbb E\|G-\bar h\|^2\le2a^2\mathbb E\|\widetilde G-\bar h\|^2+2(a-1)^2\mathbb E\|\bar h\|^2.\]
The second term cannot be removed by setting sampling variance to zero. Renaming the variable in this lemma alone does not establish the subsequent convergence proof.
checks.scope: This is a deterministic normalization error in Lemma B.7 and its dependent estimates. The corrected decomposition is not a proof of the original finite-round theorem.
checks.title: The pseudo-gradient error bound compares quantities with different scales
checks.claimContext: Equation (8) defines the server pseudo-gradient as \(G^{(t)}=\eta_c r^{(t)}\), where a client update sums its \(K\) local gradients. Appendix B.1 defines \(\bar h^{(t)}\) as a normalized average, but Lemma B.7 bounds \(\|G^{(t)}-\bar h^{(t)}\|^2\) by variance terms only.
checks.whyItMatters: Variance reduction controls randomness, not a fixed multiplicative bias between the update and its comparison gradient.
checks.checkedLocation: Lemma B.7; Equation (8); Appendix B.1 definitions of local-gradient averages

The paper already describes its chosen cheap estimator as an approximation; these problems concern the preceding exact and asymptotic claims.
checks.demonstration:
Consider a one-token, two-step masking chain with tokens \(0,1\) and mask \(M\). The terminal state is always \(M\). At the intermediate step, the model reverse kernel assigns probabilities \((1/2,2/5,1/10)\) to \((M,0,1)\). From an intermediate mask it emits either token with probability \(1/2\), while unmasked tokens are copied. All kernels are normalized and only unmask tokens. Thus the model gives \(p(x_0=0)=1/4+2/5=13/20\).

The forward process starting at \(0\) masks it with probability \(1/2\) at the intermediate step and masks it completely at the terminal step. Its two possible paths have probabilities \(1/2,1/2\), whereas the model joint probabilities of those paths and \(x_0=0\) are \(1/4,2/5\). Therefore
\[\mathrm{ELBO}=\tfrac12\log\frac{1/4}{1/2}+\tfrac12\log\frac{2/5}{1/2}=\tfrac12\log(2/5)\approx-0.458145,\]
while \(\log p(0)=\log(13/20)\approx-0.430783\). The posterior path probabilities are \((5/13,8/13)\), and
\[\log p(0)-\mathrm{ELBO}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}((1/2,1/2)\|(5/13,8/13))>0.\]
More forward-path samples converge to the displayed lower value.

For the separate marginalization claim, take data probabilities \((4/5,1/5)\) and a half-masking channel. Its exact reverse conditional returns \((4/5,1/5)\) from a mask and copies an observed token. Averaging \(p(x_0\mid x_1)\) under \(q(x_1\mid x_0)\) then gives \((9/10,3/5)\), not \((4/5,1/5)\). Correcting these two values would require multipliers \(8/9\) and \(1/3\), so a single noise-schedule weight cannot restore the identity.
checks.repair: Call the Monte Carlo quantity an ELBO estimate and retain its gap, or use a genuinely justified likelihood estimator. Replace the reverse-conditional marginalization with a valid joint-distribution identity.
checks.scope: The likelihood justification fails. The deliberately approximate cheap modifier and empirical molecular gains are not disproved.
checks.claimContext: The reference-likelihood rationale treats a path ELBO and a forward-noise average of reverse conditionals as exact marginal identities.
